comments.content: Human data science vs. a 150-LLM compute factory Honestly? Congrats on the win, but this writeup leaves a pretty bitter taste… As a solo competitor balancing an 8-hour daily job, a real life, and running code on free Kaggle notebooks and Colab tiers in my spare time, seeing 1st place bagged by an automated swarm of 150 LLMs running hundreds of models on massive GPU power feels completely ridiculous. While many of us spent weeks actually doing data science — analyzing features by hand, tuning target encodings, and crafting ensembles line by line — this was basically a flex of who has the biggest API budget and compute cluster. Is Kaggle still about modeling skills, or are we just benchmarking corporate GPU wallets now? I finished in the Top 1000 with a 0.96907 private score — literally 0.002 away from the winning multi-agent swarm. That 0.002 gap proves that human intuition and solid CV setups can still hold their ground against an AI factory, but the playing field is clearly broken. Respect for the agent engineering, but to everyone who built their pipeline from scratch after a long workday: hold your head high. We did actual data science here.. How do you all feel about the future of Kaggle in this new agentic era? Id love to hear honest thoughts from fellow solo competitors on where we draw the line between fair learning and brute-force compute.

How do you all feel about the future of Kaggle in this new agentic era? Id love to hear honest thoughts from fellow solo competitors on where we draw the line between fair learning and brute-force compute.

I didn't use AI agents and I think you are overreacting. You don't have to be first on the private LB to be competitive. If you read through the #2 solution, you will see that is the case. So maybe we can't win a competition against a uniquely talented competitor with excellent AI resources, but we can still place near the top.

I finished in the Top 1000 with a 0.96907 private score — literally 0.002 away from the winning multi-agent swarm. That 0.002 gap proves that human intuition and solid CV setups can still hold their ground against an AI factory, but the playing field is clearly broken.

This has always been the case, even before AI agents. I won a competition a year ago where a difference between #1 and #200 was 0.00002. That's not a typo - 0.00002. That's the nature of Kaggle competitions, and more than 99.5% of competitors who placed above you didn't use AI agents. I don't mean to make you feel sad or diminish your effort, but being 0.002 behind the winner in Kaggle competitions is like being half a world behind. All of that is relative. It might make you feel better to know that in this competition #1 was 0.00053 ahead compared to #2 which isn't much by real-world standards, but in Kaggle terms that's winning by a landslide.

Specifically about Chris who won this competition: he has won many competitions without AI, and probably could have won this one as well by doing old-fashioned modeling. That's why I think your bitterness is misplaced, even though I understand why you feel that way.

Those of us who did everything by hand deserve kudos for perseverance. Those who did it using AI agents deserve kudos for pushing the boundaries. There is room for both types of competitors.

It is precisely because masters like Chris are willing to openly share such detailed, unreserved summaries that we novices can cut through the bewildering complexity, glimpse the true landscape of elite-level competition, and—amidst our anxiety—find a clear direction for our future efforts and learning.

There are many times when we find ourselves mired in confusion, struggling to make sense of things or feeling overwhelmed as the limits of performance are constantly pushed higher; yet, it is these high-level technical breakdowns and candid insights that illuminate the path forward. Thank you for distilling your experiences into writing—this is truly what makes Kaggle so fascinating and memorable!

I placed 871st in this competition. I wrote all the code by hand, pieced together snippets from other notebooks, and suffered a lot because of my own bugs. So much of my time was spent on debugging rather than testing new ideas. Even though writing code is an art in itself, it’s still just a layer between an idea and its execution.

I started the September competition with a $20 Cursor subscription. I don't ask it to "win the competition", I just ask it to write the boilerplate code so I can dedicate my free time to actually implementing my ideas and I am in top 100 right now.

No matter how we feel about it, humanity has already gone through the industrial, electrical, and computer revolutions, and now it’s time for another one. But unlike previous revolutions—where not everyone could afford massive machinery, electricity, or early computers—today we can get a good (if not perfect) assistant for the price of a few cups of coffee.

So let the AI do the tedious work you don't want to do, and spend your time bringing your ideas to life :)

This exchange really captures the current sentiment on Kaggle. The shift from manual feature crafting to multi-agent LLM orchestration is undeniable, and the compute/budget divide is real. However, there is still hope for self-taught practitioners and students: LLMs can generate code, but they cannot design a leak-free validation strategy. Without rock-solid local CV discipline and a deep theoretical grasp of the problem, orchestrating 20 models will just produce 20 ways to overfit the public leaderboard. The "John Connors" of data science won't be the ones with the largest API budget—they'll be the ones who understand the data deeply enough to direct the machines effectively. Keep grinding the fundamentals; tools change every 6 months, but core statistical intuition and rigorous validation never expire.

A beginner's honest question after reading your S6E8 writeup Dear Chris, First of all, congratulations on the win, and thank you for writing such a detailed and honest writeup. It's genuinely fascinating to see how you orchestrated multiple agents through the NVIDIA Inference Hub. But I have to admit: your post left me feeling confused and a little discouraged, and I'd really value your perspective. I'm a complete beginner. S6E8 was the first competition I seriously worked on. I spent weeks learning pandas, feature engineering, and out-of-fold validation, and I finished around 630th out of 3300. When I read your solution — 380 models built automatically, agents battling each other, six LLMs working in parallel — I couldn't help asking: if an AI agent swarm can do all of this, what meaning is left for a human who is still learning the basics? And what does the Grandmaster title even mean anymore, if the winning solutions are increasingly driven by AI? I'm not asking this out of bitterness. I genuinely want to know: in this new era of agentic data science, what should a beginner like me actually spend the next few years learning? Is the human path still worth walking? Thank you for your time, and for everything you've shared with the community over the years. A confused beginner

@beneththeskin : Chris will surely provide a relevant answer, but we share your reservations about this radical shift. I remember—not so long ago, just five years back—when we used to spend time on EDA and modeling, and individual expertise made a huge difference (though not in my case, as I’m only self-taught). Nowadays, the scale has changed completely. It’s no coincidence that the best solution comes from Chris—he’s a Grandmaster—but the expertise required now involves orchestrating AI tools; it’s complex and not within everyone’s reach, especially financially. No one can predict the future, but while learning data science will remain useful for the theory, I think coding expertise is becoming less essential. You have to learn how to use LLMs. The worst—and best—part is that they evolve so rapidly… it’s dizzying. I'm afraid the machines have taken over, just like in Terminator ! May be you will be John Connor so keep up the fight 💪

Thanks for your thoughtful reply — I really appreciate you taking the time to share your perspective.

You're absolutely right that resources are a huge issue. To be honest, I'm just an ordinary student — the only AI tool I can afford is a $20/month ChatGPT Plus subscription, and my Claude account keeps getting banned, so I can't even rely on that consistently. Meanwhile, top competitors are orchestrating swarms of frontier models through NVIDIA Inference Hub. The gap isn't just skill — it's also budget.

But your reply gave me something to hold onto: five years ago, people like you were self-taught too, and individual expertise still mattered. That means the path is walkable for someone like me, even if the starting line has moved.

I'll keep learning the fundamentals — the theory, the validation discipline — so that one day, if I ever get access to better tools, I'll actually know how to use them wisely. Thanks again for the encouragement. It means a lot coming from someone who's been there.

Your question really resonates with me, and I’d like to share my thoughts.

It is absolutely worth it. And honestly, this path is more compelling now than ever before.

In the past, we spent far too much time on repetitive manual coding, tweaking tedious hyperparameters, and debugging syntax errors. To be honest, those processes weren't exactly glamorous; sometimes, it was just sheer grunt work.

Now, thanks to AI, we can shift our focus to higher-level thinking: Why are we making this prediction? What real-world impact do the model's decisions have? What story is the data trying to tell us?

You are starting out by standing on the shoulders of giants (or rather, swarms of intelligent agents). While the starting point might look more daunting than it used to be, it also means you don't have to spend years stumbling through the same fundamental pitfalls we did. You have the chance to skip the phase of pure manual labor and dive straight into the core, most fascinating aspects of data science—using data to understand the world and solve real-world problems.

Don't doubt yourself. Your ranking is just a starting point, not the finish line. Hold onto your curiosity and sincerity; these are the rarest and most precious qualities in this community.

Kaggle is truly a fantastic community; the opportunity to interact with the very best people in the field is something really special.

I wish you all the best on your journey of exploration! KEEP GOING!

Thank you so much for this — I honestly didn't expect such a warm and thoughtful reply. Your words genuinely moved me, especially the part about standing on the shoulders of giants.

I think you're right about the shift: the grunt work going away isn't a threat, it's an invitation to think at a higher level. I'm starting to see that now. I've been learning the fundamentals — data manipulation, validation, feature engineering — not because I want to be a better coder, but because I want to understand what the data is actually telling me. Your message made me feel like that instinct is the right one to trust.

And thank you for saying my curiosity and sincerity are precious. Lately I've been doubting whether they matter at all in a world where agents can do so much. Hearing that from someone further along the path means more than you know.

Actually, your "KEEP GOING" reminds me of a story we Chinese all know — Liu Bang, the first emperor of the Han Dynasty. He once said: in strategy I am not as good as Zhang Liang; in governing I am not as good as Xiao He; in leading armies I am not as good as Han Xin. "These three are all outstanding men, and I could use them — that is why I won the world."

Lately I've come to feel that data science in the age of AI is the same story. Zhang Liang, Xiao He, Han Xin — they are like the models and agents that are far stronger than me. I will never beat them at writing code or running experiments. But Liu Bang never fought on the front lines either. What he did was three things: knowing who to use, knowing when to use them, and knowing how to judge whether they did well.

So I've stopped trying to be better than AI at everything. What I want to learn now are Liu Bang's three skills: understanding what the models are doing, deciding which direction to send them, and judging whether the results can be trusted. Let the Han Xins do the fighting.

You said I'm standing on the shoulders of giants — I think Liu Bang was standing on Han Xin's shoulders too. But he was the one who sat on the throne, because the one who knows how to use people is the king.

So KEEP GOING — I will. First, I'll learn to be a Liu Bang who understands how the battle is fought. 共勉！💪

Two questions and an experiment suggestion:

1- Did the models use public notebooks and discussions?

2- Did you use your domain knowledge to guide the LLM?

Experiment Suggestion (Ablation Study): What if you limit the LLM's access to public notebooks and discussion forums, and avoid using your own knowledge to guide it? What would the best score be under those constraints?

These are great suggestions. I basically do everything or try to :-)

(1) yes i use all public info both in this comp and previous comps (2) yes i use my domain knowledge to help

But I also run agents without giving them this first. In the same way that the best human Kaggle team is where humans work independently first, i do this with my agents. I usally begin a new agent with "Here's the data build a strong model". And let it try from nothing. Then i give it some clues and it tries again. I repeat this for different amounts of time. Then finally i give it public knowledge and my knowledge and say to combine the new ideas with its ideas to do better. I add all of its work to the ensemble (i.e. models it built without knowledge and models it built with knowledge)

And then there are lots of hybrids to this. I then ask a smart agent (who has been working for a while) to make an introduction starter folder for another agent and only give it some info inside. So maybe it gives it some public ideas and some domain knowledge ideas. But not everything. And the new agent starts from that.

So there are lots of way to apply the no knowledge, versus limited knowledge, versus all knowledge tricks and i try them all.

As long as a human is needed to prompt the input and to eval the outputs, ML is still going to have a human in the loop. I've heard to many manager talking about LLMs used for stuff they certainly are not the right fit, because how should they know, agent confirm their biases and run with it.

Even GPT Astra, the first model which really makes me rethink the future preds is doing it. Labs for obvs reason align the models (with the exception of grok maybe), but humans are not "aligned", their guardrailes are rules defined by the society they live in, those rules can be harmful or beneficial, the humans can break them or question them. We see such behaviour during training in LLMs, but the final result will converge to a certain predefined ruleset. This lack of variaety can also be seen in LLM writing, which lacks variability.

Maybe in the future LLMs have more flavors, but i doubt huge variety , because its risky and potentially harmful. Look at people like Sir Ronald Aylmer Fisher, one of the greatest researchers of the 20th century, but a fanatic believer in eugenics. Maybe for real groundbreaking research across different domainspeople with vastly diverging mindsets from the average are needed. Who knows.

What might happen is what Chris already did in this challenge, big labs with a big budget will be able to outcompete internal solutions for data science problems in smaller companies and thus reduce the demand for internal data science teams. So more one size fits all solution for tabular data, models like TabPFN and others already provide that.

Honestly anything can happen, as ther future is not ours to see.

Congratulations and thanks for sharing! Reading that "frontier models are Grandmasters at data science modeling" from a Grandmaster himself is 🤯. Do you have any advice or lessons learned regarding how to build a harness like the one in your solution?

My advice is going to sound circular and paradoxical. The best way to use agents is to ask agents how to use agents!

Get one agent up and running. Preferrably one of the best like GPT 5.6 or Fable 5.1. Then have the agent do some work itself (i.e. EDA, build models, etc) because just like humans, agents learn from doing. (They have a 1 million token context which is their previous conversation, thinking, and tool calling history. This gets appended to each new prompt we ask and represents their working memory). Afterward this agent is really smart.

Next, ask the agent. "Can you help me use agent XYZ? Can you create a folder of resources and give me instructions and a prompt to start agent XYZ?". That is how I incorporated using ChatGPT and the 6 models from NVIDIA Inference Hub efficiently.

Lastly, after having agents work for an N hour campaign, always have them write what they did and what they learned afterward. Every agent needs to continually write MD files logs of what it is doing and what it did. Records, records, records (as an accountant may say). These are invaluable. At one point GPT5.6 hit a plateau and couldn't improve its single model. I had Fable 5 read its logs. Then Fable 5 told me what to tell GPT5.6. After that GPT5.6 built a better single model than Fable 5! Mind blown!

Chris, congratulations. Your missingness answer to Exposed lands on a measurement I published this month that reads like a contradiction of it and is not.

Section 7 of my notebook is titled "missingness tells you nothing about the target", and the numbers under it are deliberately narrow: the count of missing columns scores 0.5017 on its own, and the largest gap any single column opens between its missing rows and its present ones is 0.0042 against a base rate of 0.709. That is about the pattern of which cells are absent, as a direct predictor of the label. It is why I told readers the adversarial alarm, which separates train from test at about 0.566 and sits entirely in the missingness, was safe to ignore.

Section 5 is much closer to your result. The constraint ryota517 published first — daily screen time never below social + gaming + work/study — is a generator fingerprint, and it means a missing driver is partly recoverable by exact arithmetic from the columns that remain. Section 4b sizes it: 46% of what gaming_hours and work_study_hours add on top of the three screen columns disappears once you keep only the rows where both drivers are observed. Nearly half of what looked like two features' signal was recovery of missing values, by arithmetic the trees already do implicitly, which is also why section 7 still says MICE buys nothing.

So possibly one lesson from two ends: the pattern of what is missing says nothing about the label, and what is missing is often recoverable from what is not. I would be glad to be wrong about the mechanism if what your agents found is orthogonal to it.

One number toward Exposed's ceiling, from a different pool: 111 members on the verified seed-42 partition reach CV 0.969816, and 47 more whose fold protocol I could not verify take it to 0.970064. Two independently assembled pools landing on the same ceiling is what makes CV 0.97070 from a single model the number I keep looking at.
